निर्वाचन सुधारका कार्यक्रममा प्रक्रियागत सुधार गर्ने प्रतिबद्धता

ललितपुर । प्रमुख निर्वाचन आयुक्त मानबहादुर कार्कीले निर्वाचनसम्बन्धी प्राप्त सुझाव समेटेर रणनीतिक योजनाका कार्यक्रम कार्यान्वयन गर्ने प्रतिबद्धता जनाएका छन् । निर्वाचन आयोगले ललितपुरमा आयोजना गरेको चौथो रणनीतिक योजनाको मध्यावधि मूल्याङ्कनसम्बन्धी सरोकारवालासँगको परामर्श बैठकको समापनका अवसरमा उनले यस्तो प्रतिबद्धता व्यक्त गरेका हुन् ।

बैठकमा दुई वर्षभित्र सम्पन्न गर्ने लक्ष्य राखिएका ३५ कार्यक्रममध्ये १६ वटा आंशिक रूपमा कार्यान्वयन भएको र १० वटा सुरु हुन नसकेको विषयमा छलफल भएको थियो । सहभागीले कार्यक्रम असम्भव वा अनावश्यक रहेको भन्दा पनि प्रभावकारी कार्यान्वयनका लागि प्रक्रियागत सुधार आवश्यक रहेको सुझाव दिएका छन् ।

इटहरी। गृहमन्त्री सुधन गुरुङले आगामी मंसिर १७ गते विवाह गर्न लागेको सार्वजनिक गरेका छन्। स्रोतका अनुसार तमु ह्युल छोंज धीं गुरुङ राष्ट्रिय परिषद्को १५औँ केन्द्रीय पार्षदसभामा उनले विवाह गोरखामा परम्परागत गुरुङ संस्कृतिअनुसार, सादगीपूर्ण रूपमा गर्ने बताए।

गुरुङले आफ्नो पुर्खाको इतिहास, समुदायको पहिचान र मौलिक संस्कृति जोगाउन गोरखा रोजेको बताए। ऋण लिएर भए पनि भव्य भोजभतेर गर्नुपर्ने मानसिकताप्रति उनले असन्तुष्टि जनाए। पार्टी प्यालेसमा भव्य समारोह गर्न सकिने अवस्था भए पनि त्यसो नगर्ने र सीमित व्यक्ति मात्र सहभागी हुने उनको भनाइ छ। गोरखाको उक्त स्थानलाई भविष्यमा होमस्टे, स्थानीय कला–संस्कृति र पर्यटन गन्तव्यका रूपमा विकास गर्न सकिने सम्भावना पनि उनले औँल्याए। विवाहमा सरकारी प्रतिनिधि र रास्वपा सभापति रवि लामिछाने सहभागी हुने अपेक्षा गरिएको छ।

काठमाडौं । राष्ट्रिय स्वतन्त्र पार्टी (रास्वपा)ले क्यान्डिडेट क्लब समितिमा ६ सदस्य मनोनीत गरेको छ । समितिका संयोजक कविन्द्र बुर्लाकोटीको नेतृत्वमा डा. नमिता यादव, सुलभ खरेल, हिमेश पन्त, शिव यादव र पारसमणि गेलाल सदस्य रहेका छन् ।

समितिको बैठकले आगामी स्थानीय तह निर्वाचनका लागि उम्मेदवार छनोट प्रक्रियालाई व्यवस्थित, पारदर्शी र प्रभावकारी बनाउने विषयमा छलफल गरेको छ । आकांक्षी तथा आवेदकबाट आवश्यक विवरण र कागजात संकलन गर्ने विधि, बाह्य प्रवेश (ल्याटेरल इन्ट्री) को आवेदन फारम र दाबी–विरोधसम्बन्धी प्रक्रिया तयार गर्ने विषयमा पनि बैठकमा छलफल भएको छ ।

नेपाल–यूएई दोहोरो कराधान मुक्ति सम्झौताको दोस्रो चरण सम्पन्न

काठमाडौं । नेपाल र संयुक्त अरब इमिरेट्स (यूएई)बीच दोहोरो कराधान मुक्ति सम्झौता (डीटीएए) गर्ने उद्देश्यले काठमाडौंमा आयोजित द्विपक्षीय वार्ताको दोस्रो चरण सम्पन्न भएको छ। नोभेम्बर २४ देखि २६ सम्म चलेको तीनदिने वार्तामा दुवै देशका प्रतिनिधिमण्डलले कर सम्झौताका विभिन्न प्रावधानबारे छलफल गरेका हुन्।

वार्तामा नेपालका तर्फबाट आन्तरिक राजस्व विभागका महानिर्देशक डा. भीष्मकुमार भूसाल र यूएईका तर्फबाट अर्थ मन्त्रालयका अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय कर नीति विज्ञ चिराग जगदीश टानाले आ–आफ्नो प्रतिनिधिमण्डलको नेतृत्व गरेका थिए। सम्झौताले अन्तिम रूप पाएपछि दुवै देशका लगानीकर्ता दोहोरो करको भारबाट मुक्त हुने र नेपालका जलविद्युत्, नवीकरणीय ऊर्जा, पर्यटन तथा पूर्वाधार क्षेत्रमा यूएईको लगानी आकर्षित हुने विश्वास गरिएको छ।

लामिछानेले नेताहरू कार्यकर्ताबाट घेरिने र त्यही फोटोमा देखिने भएकाले त्यसलाई उम्मेदवारीको आधार बनाउन खोजिने सम्भावना औँल्याए। यस्ता तस्बिर भेटको "सुनौलो क्षण" बनेर रहन सक्ने तर टिकट पाउने प्रमाणका रूपमा प्रयोग गर्न नपाइने उनको भनाइ थियो।

उनले राजनीतिमा चलेको "झोले" शब्दमा पनि टिप्पणी गरे। रास्वपा आउनुअघि कसैलाई कांग्रेस, एमाले, माओवादीको "झोले" भनिने गरिएको र अहिले रास्वपाका कार्यकर्तालाई "खरानी घण्टे" भनिएको उनले बताए। कम्तीमा "झोले" बाट आफूहरू बाहिर निस्किए पनि त्यसभन्दा नमिठो शब्द आएको उनको टिप्पणी थियो।

करिब चार वर्षपछि फेरि आमनेसामने हुँदै मेस्सी र रोनाल्डो ?

विश्व फुटबलका दुई चर्चित खेलाडी लियोनल मेस्सी र क्रिस्टियानो रोनाल्डो करिब चार वर्षपछि फेरि एउटै मैदानमा देखिने सम्भावना बढेको छ।

अर्जेन्टिनाका पूर्व स्टार फुटबलर कार्लोस टेभेजको बिदाइ खेलका लागि दुवै खेलाडीलाई निमन्त्रणा गरिएको छ। आगामी डिसेम्बर २० मा अर्जेन्टिनाको ब्युनस आयर्सस्थित ला बम्बोनेरा रंगशालामा उक्त खेल आयोजना गर्ने तयारी छ।

मेस्सीको सहभागिता पुष्टि भएको बताइए पनि रोनाल्डोले भने आफ्नो सहभागिता पुष्टि गर्न बाँकी छ।

मेस्सी र रोनाल्डो पछिल्लो पटक सन् २०२३ को जनवरी १९ मा साउदी अरबमा आयोजित मैत्रीपूर्ण खेलमा आमनेसामने भएका थिए। रोनाल्डोले निमन्त्रणा स्वीकार गरेमा विश्वभरका फुटबलप्रेमीले यी दुई महान् खेलाडीलाई पुनः एउटै मैदानमा हेर्न पाउनेछन्।

गृहमन्त्रीको बिहेमा बालेन र रवि गोरखा जाने

काठमाडौं । गृहमन्त्री सुधन गुरुङको विवाहमा प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन्द्र शाह सहभागी हुने करिब निश्चित भएको छ । रास्वपा सभापति रवि लामिछानेले पनि बिहेमा आउने वचन दिएका छन् । गुरुङले दुवैलाई भेटेरै निम्तो दिएका थिए, लामिछानेलाई बूढानीलकण्ठस्थित निवासमै पुगेर र प्रधानमन्त्री शाहसँग हिजो राति भेटेर ।

गुरुङले सरकारका अन्य मन्त्रीहरूलाई भने नबोलाउने भएका छन् । यसअघि बोलाउने तयारी गरे तापनि अहिले उनले मनस्थिति बदलेका हुन् । गुरुङको आज काठमाडौंमा इन्गेजमेन्ट भइरहेको छ भने औपचारिक विवाह मंसिर १७ गते गोरखामा हुने निश्चित भएको छ ।

काठमाडौं । नेपाली कांग्रेसका केन्द्रीय सदस्य निलकण्ठ रिजालले पार्टीभित्रको चरम गुटबन्दीलाई पूर्णतः निस्तेज पार्न केन्द्रबाटै इमानदार कदम चाल्नुपर्ने माग गरेका छन् । सानेपामा जारी केन्द्रीय समिति बैठकमा बोल्दै उनले पार्टीका कार्यक्रम र गतिविधि भाषण र सिद्धान्तमा मात्र नभई व्यवहारमा पनि देखिनुपर्ने बताए ।

उनले नेविसंघ, तरुण दल र दलित सङ्घलगायत भातृ संस्थाका कार्यसमितिलाई छिटै पूर्णता दिई स्पष्ट समयसीमा तोकेर महाधिवेशन गर्न निर्देशन दिन र जिल्ला तथा प्रदेश अधिवेशनका मिति अविलम्ब तोक्न माग गरे । जिम्मेवारी र टिकट वितरणमा आर्थिक हैसियत हेर्ने प्रवृत्ति निरुत्साहित गर्नुपर्ने र बाटो बिराएर अन्यत्र गएका साथीलाई पूर्वाग्रहबिना मूलधारमा फर्काउन विशेष पहल गर्नुपर्ने उनको भनाइ छ ।

यसअघि पूर्वश्रममन्त्री रामेश्वर राय यादव, शेरबहादुर कुँवर र पूर्वसचिव विनोद केसी पक्राउ परिसकेका छन्। तर यही अवधिका पूर्वमन्त्री डोलप्रसाद अर्याल र शरदसिंह भण्डारी तथा पूर्वसचिव तोयम राय र केवलप्रसाद भण्डारी अनुसन्धानको दायराबाहिर छन्। शरदसिंह भण्डारी मन्त्री हुँदा मात्रै ६ पटक डलर मलेसिया पुगेको छ। एकनारायण अर्यालको बयानले अरूको भूमिका खुल्ने सीआईबी अधिकारीको भनाइ छ। मलेसियाली दूतावासका कर्मचारीको भूमिका पनि शंकास्पद देखिएको अनुसन्धानमा उल्लेख छ।

बैंकर्स संघको अध्यक्षमा रेग्मी निर्विरोध चयन

काठमाडौं । वाणिज्य बैंकहरूको साझा संस्था नेपाल बैंकर्स संघको अध्यक्षमा ग्लोबल आईएमई बैंकका प्रमुख कार्यकारी अधिकृत सुरेन्द्रराज रेग्मी चयन भएका छन् । शुक्रबार भएको संघको साधारणसभाबाट उनी निर्विरोध अध्यक्ष बनेका हुन् ।

हाल संघका उपाध्यक्ष रहेका रेग्मीलाई स्वतः अध्यक्ष बनाइएको हो । यसअघि पनि संघको अध्यक्ष स्वतः बन्ने अभ्यास रहँदै आएको थियो । संघको उपाध्यक्षमा कुमारी बैंकका सीईओ रामचन्द्र खनाल चयन भएका छन् भने सदस्यमा सिद्धार्थ बैंकका सीईओ रामेश्वर बस्याल र सानिमा बैंकका सीईओ पवन आचार्य चयन भएका छन् ।

भक्तपुर। भूमि व्यवस्था, सहकारी तथा सामान्य प्रशासनमन्त्री प्रतिभा रावलमाथि भक्तपुरको बोडे होल्डिङ सेन्टरका सुकुम्बासीले दोहोरो चरित्र देखाएको आरोप लगाएका छन्। स्रोतका अनुसार केही महिनाअघि मन्त्री रावल, गृहमन्त्री सुधन गुरुङ, महिला तथा बालबालिकामन्त्री सीता वादी र स्वास्थ्यमन्त्री निशा मेहता बोडे पुगेका थिए।

स्रोतले फेला पारेको अडियोमा रावलले सरकारले घर उपलब्ध नगराउँदासम्म सुकुम्बासीले होल्डिङ सेन्टर छाड्नु नपर्ने र समन्वय गरेर घर खोजिदिने बताएकी छन्। थापाथलीमा डोजर चलाउँदा व्यवस्थापनमा कमजोरी भएको उनले स्वीकारेकी थिइन्। तर छलफलमा सहभागी स्रोतका अनुसार सुकुम्बासीले मिडियामा गुनासो गरेकोमा उनी रुष्ट भइन् र मिडियाबाजी नगर्न चेतावनी दिइन्।

सुकुम्बासीका अनुसार सरकारले गत वैशाख १२ गते थापाथलीमा डोजर चलाएपछि उनीहरू कीर्तिपुर पुगे, असार २८ गते बाढी पसेपछि बोडे पठाइयो। आठ महिना बित्दा पनि उचित व्यवस्थापन भएको छैन, बालबालिका स्कुल जान नपाएको र धेरै बिरामी भएको उनीहरूको भनाइ छ। जिल्ला प्रशासन कार्यालय भक्तपुरले होल्डिङ सेन्टर खाली गर्न निर्देशन दिएपछि भूमि मन्त्रालयमा सोधपुछ गर्दा भक्तपुरकै प्रशासनसँग कुरा गर्न भनेर टारिएको उनीहरूले बताए।

काठमाडौँ। निजामती कर्मचारीलाई ५५ वर्ष वा ३० वर्ष सेवा पुगेपछि अनिवार्य अवकाश दिने अध्यादेश दशैँअघि चर्चामा आए पनि अहिलेसम्म आएको छैन। स्रोतका अनुसार रास्वपा सभापति रवि लामिछानेको अडानले त्यो रोकिएको हो। हाल अवकाश उमेर ५८ वर्ष छ, र प्रस्तावित व्यवस्था लागू भए करिब १० हजार कर्मचारी प्रभावित हुने अनुमान थियो।

रास्वपाको आन्तरिक राजनीति जानकार एक स्रोतका अनुसार प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन्द्र शाह अध्यादेश ल्याउने अडानमा थिए। तर कात्तिक ११ गतेको रवि–बालेन चार घण्टे छलफलमा लामिछानेले सेवा प्रवाहमा असर र रिक्त पद व्यवस्थापनको आर्थिक भार देखाउँदै विरोध गरे। ल्याइए पार्टीका सांसद नै विपक्षमा उभिन बाध्य हुने चेतावनीपछि प्रधानमन्त्री पछि हटेको स्रोतको दाबी छ।

रविनिकट एक नेताका अनुसार न्यायाधीशको "अस्वाभाविक सम्पत्ति तथा अनियमितता नियन्त्रण" सम्बन्धी अर्को अध्यादेश पनि सोही कारण रोकिएको हो। मस्यौदामा न्याय परिषद्ले हरेक वर्ष न्यायाधीशको सम्पत्ति छानबिन गर्ने, अस्वाभाविक देखिए सीआईबीले अनुसन्धान गर्ने र आर्थिक लेनदेनका आधारमा फैसला गरेको प्रमाणित भए प्रहरीले मुद्दा चलाउन सक्ने प्रावधान थियो। कानुन व्यवसायी र पूर्व महान्यायाधिवक्ताले यसलाई संविधान र लोकतन्त्रविपरीत भन्दै रोक्न सुझाएको स्रोतले बतायो। मौजुदा न्याय परिषद् ऐन, २०७३ ले नै सम्पत्ति विवरण र भ्रष्टाचार अनुसन्धानको व्यवस्था गरिसकेको छ।
गृह मन्त्रालयले अध्यागमन विभागको महानिर्देशक परिवर्तन गर्नुका साथै ६ जिल्लाका प्रमुख जिल्ला अधिकारी (सिडिओ) हेरफेर गरेको छ।

उनले कांग्रेस सभापति गगन थापासहितका व्यक्तिविरुद्ध बयान दिए छाडिदिने, नत्र फसाइदिने भन्दै धम्की दिइएको भन्ने सापकोटाकी पत्नीको उजुरीमा उल्लेखित विषयको वास्तविकता सार्वजनिक गर्न प्रधानमन्त्रीसँग माग गरेका हुन्।
हुक्काको एक सेसनमा चुरोटभन्दा ७० गुणासम्म बढी टार शरीरमा पुग्न सक्छ

रित्तो थाल बोकेर विरोध, होल्डिङ सेन्टरमा खाना बन्द

भक्तपुर । भक्तपुरको बोडेस्थित होल्डिङ सेन्टरमा बसिरहेका सुकुमबासीहरूले रित्तो थालसहित सरकारविरुद्ध प्रदर्शन गरेका छन् । सरकारले खाना दिन बन्द गरेपछि उनीहरूले रित्तो थाल बजाउँदै विरोध जनाएका हुन् ।

'हाम्रो बास खोस्न पाइँदैन, तानाशाही चलाउन पाइँदैन' भन्दै उनीहरूले हातमा प्लेकार्ड लिएका छन् । सरकारले होल्डिङ सेन्टर खाली गर्न दिउँसो २ बजेसम्मको समयसीमा तोकेको थियो । काठमाडौं उपत्यकाका नदी किनारका बस्ती हटाइएपछि विस्थापित भएका परिवार यहाँ आश्रय लिइरहेका थिए ।

बागलुङको ढोरपाटनमा पुग्यो राष्ट्रिय ग्रिडको विद्युत्

काठमाडौं । नेपाल विद्युत् प्राधिकरणले बागलुङको पर्यटकीय क्षेत्र ढोरपाटन उपत्यकामा राष्ट्रिय प्रसारण प्रणालीको विद्युत् पुर्याएको छ । मोतीपुरबाट सन्धिखर्क, तम्घास र पौंदीअमराई हुँदै बुर्तिवाङसम्मको १३२ केभी प्रसारण लाइन र बुर्तिवाङ सबस्टेसनमार्फत आपूर्ति सुरु भएको हो ।

बुर्तिवाङबाट नवी हुँदै छेन्तुङसम्मको ११ केभी फिडर सञ्चालनमा आएसँगै करिब १३ वटा वितरण ट्रान्सफर्मर चार्ज भएका छन् । यसअघि लघुजलविद्युत् प्रयोग गर्दै आएका उपभोक्ताले अब राष्ट्रिय ग्रिडको विद्युत् पाउनेछन्, जसले न्यून भोल्टेजको समस्या समाधान गर्ने अपेक्षा छ ।

वैकल्पिक व्यवस्था नगरी सुकुमवासी नहटाउन आग्रह

काठमाडौं । उज्यालो नेपाल पार्टीका अध्यक्ष कुलमान घिसिङले सुकुमवासी परिवारलाई वैकल्पिक आवासको व्यवस्था नगरी विस्थापित नगर्न सरकारसँग आग्रह गरेका छन् । काठमाडौं उपत्यकाका नदी किनारबाट विस्थापित भएका परिवारलाई आश्रय दिइएको भक्तपुरको बोडेस्थित कृषि विकास बैंकको तालिम केन्द्र खाली गर्न निर्देशन दिइएको सन्दर्भमा उनले यस्तो आग्रह गरेका हुन् ।

जाडोको मौसममा सुरक्षित आवासको सुनिश्चितताबिना पुनः विस्थापित गर्नु उचित नहुने उनको भनाइ छ । विशेषगरी बालबालिका, ज्येष्ठ नागरिक, महिला तथा अशक्त व्यक्तिको अवस्थालाई संवेदनशीलतापूर्वक विचार गर्नुपर्ने भन्दै उनले वैकल्पिक आवासको व्यवस्था नहुन्जेल आश्रयस्थल खाली गराउने निर्णय स्थगित गर्न र दीर्घकालीन तथा न्यायपूर्ण समाधान खोज्न सरकारसँग आग्रह गरेका छन् ।

शिक्षकको पेन्सनमा अन्योल, अर्थको पुरानो पत्रले हलचल

रुपन्देही । २०७५ सालपछि स्थायी नियुक्ति भएका शिक्षकको निवृत्तिभरण (पेन्सन) मा कानुनी अस्पष्टता देखिँदा शिक्षक वृत्तमा अन्योल बढेको छ । योगदानमा आधारित पेन्सन प्रणाली लागू गर्ने कानुनी व्यवस्था भए पनि शिक्षकको तलबबाट योगदान रकम कट्टा गर्ने र सरकारले रकम थपेर कोषमा जम्मा गर्ने प्रक्रिया अझै सुरु भएको छैन ।

अर्थ मन्त्रालयको २०८३ असार १२ को पुरानो पत्र सार्वजनिक भएपछि विवाद चुलिएको छ । नेपाल शिक्षक संघका महासचिव ज्ञानेन्द्र रावलले कोष नै नकाटिएको अवस्थामा पुरानो मितिबाट प्रणाली लागू भएको मान्न नसकिने बताएका छन् । शिक्षकहरूले शिक्षा र अर्थ मन्त्रालयबीच समन्वय गरी अन्योल हटाउन र पेन्सन लागू हुने मितिबारे स्पष्ट निर्णय गर्न माग गरेका छन् ।

कृष्णमायाको ध्यान भने एउटै कुरामा थियो — कति बेला २ बज्छ र सरकारले के गर्छ?

बिहान ९ बज्यो। कोही आएनन्।

१० बजे पनि उनले गेटतिर हेरिन्। कोही देखिनन्।

पूर्वउपप्रधानमन्त्री टोपबहादुर रायमाझीले जेलमुक्त भएपछि पहिलोपटक गृहजिल्ला अर्घाखाँची पुगेर आफूलाई नक्कली भुटानी शरणार्थी प्रकरणमा फसाइएको दाबी गरेका छन्। करिब साढे तीन वर्ष जेल बसेका उनले स्वागत कार्यक्रमहरूमा कारागारका ७० प्रतिशत कैदी निर्दोष रहेको र समयक्रमसँगै सबै कुरा खुल्दै जाने बताए।

अदालतले उनलाई ठगी, संगठित अपराध र राज्यविरुद्धको कसुरमा चार वर्ष कैद र ४० हजार जरिवाना गरेको थियो। ६५ वर्ष पुगेपछि २५ प्रतिशत छुट पाएका उनी कात्तिक २६ गते रिहा भएका हुन्। उनले "तेरो र मेरो पार्टी" भन्न जरुरी नभएको र नयाँ दलको लक्षण पनि राम्रो नदेखिएको टिप्पणी गरे। पत्थरकोट, ठाडा र सुपादेउराली परिसरमा उनलाई स्वागत गर्नेको लर्को लागेको थियो।
बार काउन्सिलले किन ल्यायो कुलिङ अफ पिरियड?

प्रहरीले नै लेखेको कुरा पढ्न लगाएर अडिओ बनाएको इनम सापकोटाको आरोप
-
प्रहरीले आफूलाई फसाउन मोबाइल फोनमा छेडखानी गरी झूटा प्रमाण सिर्जना गरेको र अनुसन्धानका सामग्री बाहिर चुहाएर आफ्नो मिडिया ट्रायल गरेको आरोप पनि उनले लगाएका छन्।

काठमाडौँ । प्रहरी हिरासतमा रहेका इनम सापकोटाको जीवन रक्षा र मानव अधिकार संरक्षणको माग गर्दै राष्ट्रिय मानव अधिकार आयोगमा उजुरी परेको छ । उनकी पत्नी कविता पाण्डेले शुक्रबार आयोगको ललितपुरस्थित कार्यालयमा उजुरी दर्ता गराएकी हुन् ।

पाँच पृष्ठ लामो निवेदनमा सापकोटालाई विमानस्थलबाट नियन्त्रणमा लिएर आँखामा कालोपट्टी बाँधी अज्ञात स्थलमा राखिएको, मानसिक यातना दिइएको र विभिन्न उच्चपदस्थ व्यक्तिविरुद्ध बयान दिन दबाब दिएको आरोप लगाइएको छ ।

निवेदनअनुसार पूर्वप्रधानन्यायाधीश चोलेन्द्रशमशेर जबरा, कांग्रेस सभापति गगन थापा, नेता तथा व्यवसायी उमेश श्रेष्ठ, व्यवसायी मीनबहादुर गुरुङ, नवीन तुलाधर र सर्वोच्च अदालतका केही न्यायाधीशविरुद्ध बयान दिन दबाब दिइएको थियो । बयान नदिए आफू र परिवारलाई खतरा हुने तथा झुटा मुद्दामा लामो समय जेल बस्नुपर्ने धम्की दिइएको पाण्डेको दाबी छ ।

सापकोटालाई आफूले नबोलेका कुरा लेखिएको कागजमा हस्ताक्षर गर्न दबाब दिइएको र सार्वजनिक भएको अडियोसमेत त्यही सामग्री काँटछाँट गरेर तयार पारिएको निवेदनमा उल्लेख छ । प्रहरीले नियन्त्रणमा लिएको मोबाइल अनधिकृत व्यक्तिलाई दिएको र एआईबाट सिर्जित कागजातलाई समेत प्रमाणका रूपमा प्रस्तुत गर्न खोजिएको आरोप पनि लगाइएको छ ।

THE OCEAN'S INTERNET CABLES COULD BECOME A LIFELINE FOR ORCAS. 🐋🌊

Scientists are testing a remarkable way to listen for whales using the same fiber-optic cables that carry internet data across the ocean floor.

With a technology called Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS), tiny vibrations in the cables can be detected and converted into sound. Researchers have already recorded orca calls along a test cable in the Pacific Northwest.

The technology could help scientists locate orcas, understand their movements, and potentially alert ships when whales are nearby—giving vessels a chance to slow down or avoid them.

It is still being developed, but this could turn the internet's underwater infrastructure into a powerful tool for protecting marine life.

The real story: On Saturday, October 17, 2026, a group of Eastern Tropical Pacific orcas that came from Mexico killed an adult fin whale off San Diego, California. Naturalist Nicole Schriber captured footage for Gone Whale Watching San Diego, whose owner, Dominic Biagini, estimated the whale was "pushing 60 feet." Fin whales are not routinely attacked by orcas, mainly because of their size and speed. Another report, published October 24, says orcas were seen with a smaller fin whale on Friday, October 23. Source: The Spokesman-Review, October 17, 2026; follow-up from AOL, October 24, 2026.

Off San Diego, whale watchers are used to seeing common dolphins. On Saturday, October 17, 2026, they saw something far rarer.

Naturalist Nicole Schriber captured footage for Gone Whale Watching San Diego as a group of Eastern Tropical Pacific orcas, a population that came up from Mexico, killed an adult fin whale. The company's owner, Dominic Biagini, estimated the whale was "pushing 60 feet." Fin whales can reach about 85 feet and are the second-largest animals on the planet, after blue whales. They are not routinely attacked by orcas, mainly because of their size and speed.

These orcas had been seen several times off San Diego in the weeks before, mostly hunting common dolphins. The company said it would release more footage soon.

Then, on Friday, October 23, another report from AOL said orcas were seen again with a fin whale, smaller than the first, which they raised to the surface beside the 139-foot historic sailing vessel Yacht America. The orcas also performed a spyhop, rising head-first out of the water to look at the boat. It was unclear, the report says, whether the orcas were "prey sharing," a behavior this population is known for.

One of the Navy's most futuristic warships may be getting a whole new purpose.

The US Navy is planning to turn the Zumwalt-class destroyer USS Michael Monsoor into a hypersonic strike ship. The plan: pull out the two giant deck cannons it was built around, and drop in a 600-ton module with four launch tubes holding up to twelve Conventional Prompt Strike hypersonic rounds, conventional, not nuclear, each able to travel at more than five times the speed of sound.

Here's the twist. The Zumwalt's big guns were abandoned years ago because their special ammunition became wildly expensive, leaving these advanced ships with main guns they couldn't really use. Repurposing them for hypersonics finally gives them a mission that fits.

But there's an honest catch worth knowing. A government watchdog report says US industry can currently build only about six or seven of these hypersonic missiles a year, and it takes twelve to fill one ship. America can design the technology; the harder part is producing it at scale. It's a reminder that real military strength isn't just invention, it's the factories and workers behind it. (Plans are still conditional, with work penciled in for 2028 to 2030.)

The Pentagon agreed to all four GAO fixes and is targeting a full F-35 parts inventory by March 2027.

What it does show is that the race to put capable drones on and around aircraft carriers is heating up on both sides of the Pacific, with the US MQ-25 as the benchmark others appear to be measuring against.

A Nazi commandant ordered him to hand over the Jewish American POWs.
Master Sgt. Roddie Edmonds replied: “We are all Jews here.”

In January 1945, Master Sgt. Roddie Edmonds was the highest-ranking American noncommissioned officer at a German POW camp.

A Nazi commandant demanded that all Jewish American prisoners step forward.
Edmonds ordered every man in the barracks to stand instead.

When the commandant pressed him, Edmonds said, “We are all Jews here.”

The officer put a pistol to Edmonds’ head and demanded he identify the Jewish soldiers.
Edmonds refused.
He told him that if he shot, he would have to shoot all of them — and that he would be prosecuted for war crimes.

The commandant backed down.

Edmonds’ actions saved an estimated 200 Jewish American POWs.

He never sought recognition. The story only fully came to light decades later through the testimony of the men he protected.

Some stands are taken quietly, under a gun, and still change everything.

America is one step closer to retiring tankers older than the crews who fly them.

The US Air Force has ordered its final batch of KC-46 Pegasus tankers under Boeing's original contract, a $2.82 billion buy for 15 more jets. Tankers are the quiet backbone of American airpower: they refuel fighters, bombers and cargo planes in midair so they can reach fights across the globe. The KC-46 is built to replace the KC-135 Stratotanker, a jet whose fleet was largely built in the 1950s and early '60s.

The Air Force has received 116 Pegasus tankers so far and wants 263 in all to fully replace those Cold War-era aircraft. It's not been a cheap or easy program, Boeing has absorbed more than $7 billion in losses under a fixed-price deal, and the jet has worked through issues with its refueling boom and camera system, with fixes and a 20%-plus boost in availability planned by 2030.

It's a reminder of how much of America's global reach rides on these unsung aircraft, and of the long, costly work of keeping that reach modern.

America's newest Eagle has landed in the Pacific.

The first F-15EX Eagle II fighters have arrived at Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, Japan. Two are on the ground so far, the leading edge of a planned 36 that will replace the base's aging fleet of 48 F-15C and F-15D jets, Eagles that have guarded the Western Pacific for decades.

It's a real step up. Where the old F-15C was built almost purely for air-to-air combat, the F-15EX is a true multirole fighter, with modern avionics and networking, a bigger payload, and more speed and range than earlier Eagles. Pilots of the 67th Fighter Squadron spent about a year and a half training to make the jump.

Kadena is often called the "keystone of the Pacific," and the 18th Wing commander called the new jets "just another sign of the United States Air Force's commitment" to the mission there, and to flying alongside Japanese Air Self-Defense Force Eagles based nearby. Fifty years on, the legendary F-15 is still standing watch, in its newest and most capable form yet.

Most of a free-fall jump happens on the ground. Twenty-three years ago this Thanksgiving, about 600 soldiers from the 1st Armored Division and the 82nd Airborne Division sat down for turkey and ham at the Bob Hope Dining Facility at Baghdad International Airport. None of them knew who their guest of honor would be.

Junior sailors move into unaccompanied housing, and more senior sailors into lodging rooms, at the carrier's homeport of Yokosuka, Japan.

The point is rest. After months at sea in cramped, stacked racks shared with dozens of others, the Navy wants returning sailors to have a real room to recuperate in. It ties into the Chief of Naval Operations' "No Sailor Lives Afloat" initiative to improve how sailors are housed.

The George Washington spent about three months in the Middle East before being relieved and heading home. Looking after the people who serve, right down to where they sleep after a long deployment, is the kind of thing that keeps a fleet strong.

American soldiers built their own air-cargo line across Europe, and it's a great example of military ingenuity at work.

It's called "Demon Express." Set up in June by the 1st Combat Aviation Brigade, 1st Infantry Division, it uses CH-47F Chinook helicopters to shuttle maintenance equipment, parts and crews between Forward Operating Site Powidz in Poland and Illesheim Army Airfield in Germany. That run used to take about half a day by road. By Chinook, it's roughly three hours, about 75% faster.

Every month, the flights move tens of thousands of pounds of gear and dozens of personnel, all to cut maintenance downtime and keep the brigade's aircraft ready to fly. "Every Demon Express mission that we run is critical to some aspect of maintenance," said 1st Lt. Cole Dack. The toughest obstacle right now is winter icing along the route, so the crews work with Air Force weather specialists to pick safe flight windows.

As the brigade commander put it, this is a unit "with a requirement to fly to accomplish our mission." Behind every ready aircraft is a chain of parts, people and hard work, and in Europe, a lot of that chain now flies.

The Ultimate Stand: Gary Gordon And Randy Shughart At Super Six Four
The Radio Requests From Above On October 3, 1993, during the intense street fighting of the Battle of Mogadishu, Black Hawk helicopter Super Six Four, piloted by Chief Warrant Officer Michael Durant, was struck by an RPG and crashed into a hostile neighborhood. Circling overhead in Super Six Two, Delta Force sniper team leader Master Sgt. Gary Gordon and his partner Sgt. 1st Class Randy Shughart watched armed hostile crowds numbering in the thousands converge on the downed wreckage. With no ground rescue convoy capable of reaching the site in time, Gordon radioed command requesting permission to be inserted on foot to protect the wounded crew. Command denied the request twice, warning that two men could not survive against an entire armed city. Fierce Defense And The Final Weapon Infilled roughly 100 meters away, Gordon and Shughart fought their way through an intense maze of shanties under heavy fire to reach the wreckage. At 32,000 feet over Pennsylvania, an ordinary Tuesday morning flight suddenly became every aviator’s worst nightmare.

A metal fatigue fracture inside the left CFM56 engine sheared off a fan blade at cruising speed. Within milliseconds, the entire cowling disintegrated into flying shrapnel, puncturing the fuselage and blowing out a cabin window at row 14.

The cockpit erupted into instant chaos. Rapid decompression roared through the airframe, dropping cabin temperature below zero, flooding the cockpit with white vapor, and filling the air with deafening wind noise. The Boeing 737 shuddered violently, banking hard to 41 degrees with only one operational engine and zero internal communication back to the flight attendants.

In command was Captain Tammie Jo Shults, backed by First Officer Darren Ellisor.

Decades before flying commercial routes, Shults was breaking barriers in naval aviation as one of the first women to pilot the supersonic F/A-18 Hornet and fly tactical profiles in the A-7 Corsair II. She had spent years mastering emergency procedures on pitching carrier decks in pitch darkness, conditioning her nervous system to replace fear with immediate muscle memory.

While cockpit alarms blared and the airframe fought severe aerodynamic drag, Shults keyed her microphone to Philadelphia air traffic control. Her voice did not crack. Her cadence did not waver. She sounded like someone ordering a morning coffee.

"Southwest 1380 has an engine fire," she transmitted calmly. "We would like to descend."

When the controller asked whether the aircraft was actively on fire, her reply was cold steel.

"No, it is not on fire, but part of it is missing. They say there is a hole and someone went out."

Wrestling asymmetric thrust and flap damage, Shults manually stabilized the crippled airliner, brought it down on runway 27L at 165 knots, and safely delivered 148 souls home.

“WE SPENT 52 DAYS IN THE DMZ MEAT GRINDER. HALF MY COMPANY WAS KILLED OR WOUNDED BEFORE MY 18TH BIRTHDAY.” — Vietnam Marine Machine Gunner Johnnie Clark on The Shawn Ryan Show.

Combat Marine machine gunner and author Johnnie Clark shares harrowing recollections of surviving Operation Prairie in the demilitarized zone during the Vietnam War.

In his own words:

“I enlisted in the Marine Corps as a teenager and was immediately sent up north to the DMZ as an M60 machine gunner—the most dangerous job in the infantry.

We were thrown into Operation Prairie fighting the North Vietnamese Army in the jungle. For 52 straight days, we were under constant mortar barrages, sniper fire, and mass human-wave assaults.

You’re sleeping in muddy trenches filled with leeches and trench foot, covered in the blood of boys you went through bootcamp with.

In less than two months, over half my company was killed or wounded. I watched my squad leader take a round right through the chest while handing me ammunition.

When you survive that kind of unrelenting carnage at 18 years old, a piece of your youth dies in that jungle forever. You spend the rest of your life trying to justify why God chose you to walk off that hill when so many better men stayed behind.”

In one of the most explosive interviews in the history of The Shawn Ryan Show (Episode #252), former DEVGRU assaulter Matt Bissonnette—who authored No Easy Day under the pen name "Mark Owen"—broke his 12-year silence on the raid that killed Osama bin Laden and the federal government's relentless legal retaliation against him.

In his own words:

“I’ve been fighting my own government for 12 years.

Three weeks after the Bin Laden mission, we go to Leon Panetta’s retirement ceremony in Langley, Virginia. He gets off stage and literally brings over Hollywood producers and directors, saying, ‘Hey look, they’re going to make you famous.’ They had full White House and CIA access to make Zero Dark Thirty.

I was an enlisted guy. I’m sitting there watching every single politician and leader from Washington talk about their heroic decisions for reelection campaigns, while none of the 24 operators who actually kicked the doors got any credit.

When I wrote No Easy Day, the government immediately came after me with unlimited attorneys. In the end, they admitted there was nothing classified in the book—they just wanted all the money back.

I spent $1.5 million of that money defending myself against their accusations. The government said, ‘We want that back too.’

So they put me on a garnishment plan: $3,800 every single month for the next 15 years. They told me if I miss one payment, they’ll charge me back taxes and prosecute me again.

I served this country for 14 straight combat tours. When I got out, I received a plaque with my first name misspelled—one ‘T’ in Matt. And now they want me paying them back for longer than I even wore the uniform.”

Washington politicians and intelligence officials handed classified access to Hollywood filmmakers for Zero Dark Thirty, yet when an enlisted SEAL who kicked the doors in Abbottabad wrote about his own experience, the federal government stripped every penny he earned and put him on a 15-year garnishment plan.

A Nazi commandant ordered him to hand over the Jewish American POWs.
Master Sgt. Roddie Edmonds replied: “We are all Jews here.”

In January 1945, Master Sgt. Roddie Edmonds was the highest-ranking American noncommissioned officer at a German POW camp.

A Nazi commandant demanded that all Jewish American prisoners step forward.
Edmonds ordered every man in the barracks to stand instead.

When the commandant pressed him, Edmonds said, “We are all Jews here.”

The officer put a pistol to Edmonds’ head and demanded he identify the Jewish soldiers.
Edmonds refused.
He told him that if he shot, he would have to shoot all of them — and that he would be prosecuted for war crimes.

The commandant backed down.

Edmonds’ actions saved an estimated 200 Jewish American POWs.

He never sought recognition. The story only fully came to light decades later through the testimony of the men he protected.

Some stands are taken quietly, under a gun, and still change everything.

The sun is going down over the Mojave, and the jump hasn't started yet. On 18 July 2025, Marines with 2d Reconnaissance Battalion, 2d Marine Division, got ready for a night free-fall jump at the Marine Corps Air-Ground Combat Center in Twentynine Palms, California, during Service Level Training Exercise 4-25.

Most of a free-fall jump happens on the ground. Before anyone boards the C-130, rigs get checked and rechecked, straps are adjusted, oxygen systems are inspected, and the numbers that will decide where every jumper lands get worked out and verified. At night, over the desert, there's no room for mistakes. Everyone has to trust their own rig, the man packing next to them, and the team in the back of the aircraft.

That's the side of Recon most people never see. The skill that gets a team behind the lines quietly is built on hours of unglamorous preparation like this. The jump itself is the shortest part of the night.

Twenty-three years ago this Thanksgiving, about 600 soldiers from the 1st Armored Division and the 82nd Airborne Division sat down for turkey and ham at the Bob Hope Dining Facility at Baghdad International Airport. None of them knew who their guest of honor would be.

President George W. Bush had flown into Baghdad under darkness and tight secrecy. Almost no one outside a small circle knew about it, including most of the White House press corps. When he stepped out from behind a curtain, the room erupted. "I was just looking for a warm meal somewhere," he told them. Then he helped serve dinner and shook hands down the line. He spent about two and a half hours on the ground before flying out again.

The visit came as the war in Iraq was entering a harder phase and coalition casualties were climbing. For the soldiers in that dining hall, it was one Thanksgiving far from home that they wouldn't forget.

The Ultimate Stand: Gary Gordon And Randy Shughart At Super Six Four
The Radio Requests From Above On October 3, 1993, during the intense street fighting of the Battle of Mogadishu, Black Hawk helicopter Super Six Four, piloted by Chief Warrant Officer Michael Durant, was struck by an RPG and crashed into a hostile neighborhood. Circling overhead in Super Six Two, Delta Force sniper team leader Master Sgt. Gary Gordon and his partner Sgt. 1st Class Randy Shughart watched armed hostile crowds numbering in the thousands converge on the downed wreckage. With no ground rescue convoy capable of reaching the site in time, Gordon radioed command requesting permission to be inserted on foot to protect the wounded crew. Command denied the request twice, warning that two men could not survive against an entire armed city. On their third urgent request, knowing rescue was hours away, command relented and cleared them for insertion

Fierce Defense And The Final Weapon Infilled roughly 100 meters away, Gordon and Shughart fought their way through an intense maze of shanties under heavy fire to reach the wreckage. They pulled Durant, who had sustained a broken leg and crushed vertebrae, from the crushed cockpit alongside his crew, moving them behind the fuselage to establish a perimeter. Fighting with bolt-action sniper rifles and sidearms, both snipers held off waves of militia until their ammunition ran dry. After Shughart fell, Gordon salvaged a rifle with the remaining rounds, handed it to the injured pilot with the parting words, “Good luck,” and went back into the fight with only his sidearm until he was overwhelmed

First Medals Of Honor Since Vietnam The stand of Gordon and Shughart delayed the armed crowd long enough to keep Durant alive until he was taken prisoner and ultimately released 11 days later. On May 23, 1994, both snipers were posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor, becoming the first service members to receive the nation’s highest military decoration since the Vietnam War

At 32,000 feet over Pennsylvania, an ordinary Tuesday morning flight suddenly became every aviator’s worst nightmare.

A metal fatigue fracture inside the left CFM56 engine sheared off a fan blade at cruising speed. Within milliseconds, the entire cowling disintegrated into flying shrapnel, puncturing the fuselage and blowing out a cabin window at row 14.

The cockpit erupted into instant chaos. Rapid decompression roared through the airframe, dropping cabin temperature below zero, flooding the cockpit with white vapor, and filling the air with deafening wind noise. The Boeing 737 shuddered violently, banking hard to 41 degrees with only one operational engine and zero internal communication back to the flight attendants.

In command was Captain Tammie Jo Shults, backed by First Officer Darren Ellisor.

Decades before flying commercial routes, Shults was breaking barriers in naval aviation as one of the first women to pilot the supersonic F/A-18 Hornet and fly tactical profiles in the A-7 Corsair II. She had spent years mastering emergency procedures on pitching carrier decks in pitch darkness, conditioning her nervous system to replace fear with immediate muscle memory.

While cockpit alarms blared and the airframe fought severe aerodynamic drag, Shults keyed her microphone to Philadelphia air traffic control. Her voice did not crack. Her cadence did not waver. She sounded like someone ordering a morning coffee.

"Southwest 1380 has an engine fire," she transmitted calmly. "We would like to descend."

When the controller asked whether the aircraft was actively on fire, her reply was cold steel.

"No, it is not on fire, but part of it is missing. They say there is a hole and someone went out."

Wrestling asymmetric thrust and flap damage, Shults manually stabilized the crippled airliner, brought it down on runway 27L at 165 knots, and safely delivered 148 souls home.

When catastrophe strikes at 32,000 feet, how does military flight discipline prepare pilots for split-second commercial emergencies?

Combat Marine machine gunner and author Johnnie Clark shares harrowing recollections of surviving Operation Prairie in the demilitarized zone during the Vietnam War.

In his own words:

“I enlisted in the Marine Corps as a teenager and was immediately sent up north to the DMZ as an M60 machine gunner—the most dangerous job in the infantry.

We were thrown into Operation Prairie fighting the North Vietnamese Army in the jungle. For 52 straight days, we were under constant mortar barrages, sniper fire, and mass human-wave assaults.

You’re sleeping in muddy trenches filled with leeches and trench foot, covered in the blood of boys you went through bootcamp with.

In less than two months, over half my company was killed or wounded. I watched my squad leader take a round right through the chest while handing me ammunition.

When you survive that kind of unrelenting carnage at 18 years old, a piece of your youth dies in that jungle forever. You spend the rest of your life trying to justify why God chose you to walk off that hill when so many better men stayed behind.”

Supporters emphasize that creating protected categories for biological women is essential to ensuring female athletes continue to have equal access to podium finishes, championship titles, and athletic college scholarships. In his own words:

“I’ve been fighting my own government for 12 years.

Three weeks after the Bin Laden mission, we go to Leon Panetta’s retirement ceremony in Langley, Virginia. He gets off stage and literally brings over Hollywood producers and directors, saying, ‘Hey look, they’re going to make you famous.’ They had full White House and CIA access to make Zero Dark Thirty.

I was an enlisted guy. I’m sitting there watching every single politician and leader from Washington talk about their heroic decisions for reelection campaigns, while none of the 24 operators who actually kicked the doors got any credit.

When I wrote No Easy Day, the government immediately came after me with unlimited attorneys. In the end, they admitted there was nothing classified in the book—they just wanted all the money back.

I spent $1.5 million of that money defending myself against their accusations. The government said, ‘We want that back too.’

So they put me on a garnishment plan: $3,800 every single month for the next 15 years. They told me if I miss one payment, they’ll charge me back taxes and prosecute me again.

I served this country for 14 straight combat tours. When I got out, I received a plaque with my first name misspelled—one ‘T’ in Matt. And now they want me paying them back for longer than I even wore the uniform.”

Washington politicians and intelligence officials handed classified access to Hollywood filmmakers for Zero Dark Thirty, yet when an enlisted SEAL who kicked the doors in Abbottabad wrote about his own experience, the federal government stripped every penny he earned and put him on a 15-year garnishment plan.

A Nazi commandant ordered him to hand over the Jewish American POWs.
Master Sgt. Roddie Edmonds replied: “We are all Jews here.”

In January 1945, Master Sgt. Roddie Edmonds was the highest-ranking American noncommissioned officer at a German POW camp.

A Nazi commandant demanded that all Jewish American prisoners step forward.
Edmonds ordered every man in the barracks to stand instead.

When the commandant pressed him, Edmonds said, “We are all Jews here.”

The officer put a pistol to Edmonds’ head and demanded he identify the Jewish soldiers.
Edmonds refused.
He told him that if he shot, he would have to shoot all of them — and that he would be prosecuted for war crimes.

The commandant backed down.

Edmonds’ actions saved an estimated 200 Jewish American POWs.

He never sought recognition. The story only fully came to light decades later through the testimony of the men he protected.

Some stands are taken quietly, under a gun, and still change everything.

Robert Lewis Howard (July 11, 1939 – December 23, 2009) was a highly decorated United States Army Special Forces officer and Medal of Honor recipient of the Vietnam War.

He was wounded 14 times over 54 months of combat, was awarded the Medal of Honor, eight Purple Hearts, a Distinguished Service Cross, a Silver Star, and four Bronze Stars.

He was nominated for the Medal of Honor three separate times over a 13-month period but received lesser medals for the first two nominations, which were for actions performed in Cambodia, where the U.S. was fighting covertly. He received the Medal of Honor for his actions on November 16, 1967, in North Vietnam, his third nomination.

He retired from the US Army after 36 years of service as a full colonel, and the most highly decorated service member on active duty.

He died as a result of pancreatic cancer and was buried at Arlington National Cemetery on February 22, 2010.

At the time of his death he was the most decorated living Medal of Honor recipient.

CITATION: For conspicuous gallantry and intrepidity in action at the risk of his life above and beyond the call of duty. 1st Lt. Howard (then SFC) distinguished himself while serving as platoon sergeant of an American-Vietnamese platoon which was on a mission to rescue a missing American soldier in enemy controlled territory in the Republic of Vietnam. The platoon had left its helicopter landing zone and was moving out on its mission when it was attacked by an estimated 2-company force. During the initial engagement, 1st Lt. Howard was wounded and his weapon destroyed by a grenade explosion. 1st Lt. Howard saw his platoon leader had been wounded seriously and was exposed to fire. Although unable to walk and weaponless, 1st Lt. Howard unhesitatingly crawled through a hail of fire to retrieve his wounded leader. As 1st Lt. Howard was administering first aid and removing the officer's equipment, an enemy bullet struck 1 of the ammunition pouches on the lieutenant's belt, detonating several magazines of ammunition. 1st Lt. Howard momentarily sought cover and then, realizing that he must rejoin the platoon, which had been disorganized by the enemy attack, he again began dragging the seriously wounded officer toward the platoon area. Through his outstanding example of indomitable courage and bravery, 1st Lt. Howard was able to rally the platoon into an organized defense force. With complete disregard for his safety, 1st Lt. Howard crawled from position to position, administering first aid to the wounded, giving encouragement to the defenders, and directing their fire on the encircling enemy. For 3 1⁄2 hours, 1st Lt. Howard's small force and supporting aircraft successfully repulsed enemy attacks and finally were in sufficient control to permit the landing of rescue helicopters. 1st Lt. Howard personally supervised the loading of his men and did not leave the bullet-swept landing zone until all were aboard safely. 1st Lt. Howard's gallantry in action, his complete devotion to the welfare of his men at the risk of his life, were in keeping with the highest traditions of the military service and reflect great credit on himself, his unit, and the U.S. Army.

Died April 10, 2003 Serving During Operation Iraqi Freedom

39, of Ossian, Iowa; assigned to 1st Battalion, 5th Marine Regiment, Camp Pendleton, Calif.; killed April 10 in northern Baghdad while engaging enemy forces.

In the face of danger, most would run toward safety. Yet, when then-Lance Cpl. Corbin was faced with such a decision, he ran toward peril and possible death – braving intense enemy fire to help injured comrades.

Corbin, a medium tactical vehicle replacement driver, and his unit were stationed in the Al Anbar province to help secure and stabilize the volatile area. They had just finished several days of routine patrol on May 7, 2005, and were returning to the Haditha Dam when they got the call.

A platoon from their battalion was under attack on the east side of the Euphrates River and needed support to block the insurgents' retreat. Corbin's team – a quick reaction force (QRF) – quickly responded to the call. As the QRF crept toward the attack site, there was an unnatural stillness in the air.

“There was no one out, nothing moving,” Corbin later told the Marine Corps Times.

With every nerve on alert, the QRF kept driving toward the ambush site, knowing there were injured Marines that needed them. Suddenly, a vehicle laden with IEDs sped toward the convoy and blew up between two of the Humvees. Another blast followed as enemy fighters began firing upon the group.

The swift attack devastated Corbin's team – three of the four vehicles were severely damaged, and 11 of 16 Marines were injured or killed. Taking control of the situation, Corbin immediately repositioned his vehicle between the insurgents' fire and the wounded Marines. As he radioed in the situation, he began directing a counter-attack.

As those that could return fire, Corbin began recovering dead and wounded personnel and moving them toward safety. Running through the line of fire, Corbin grabbed his wounded patrol leader and threw him over his shoulder. He then sprinted back to his Humvee, firing at enemies as he ran. Corbin ran back and forth several times through the kill zone, moving everyone he could out of the withering fire and loaded them into his vehicle.

Arming every able Marine with as much ammunition and weapons as they could hold, Corbin drove his severely damaged Humvee through the kill zone toward the battle aid station. Even injured, the Marines were a deadly force to be reckoned with. Insurgents continued to pelt the rumbling truck with mortars and small-arms fire, but the Marines made it to safety.

Corbin's quick actions ensured that no Marines were killed after that initial attack. For his leadership, Corbin was awarded the Navy Cross on April 12, 2006.

At 32,000 feet over Pennsylvania, an ordinary Tuesday morning flight suddenly became every aviator’s worst nightmare.

A metal fatigue fracture inside the left CFM56 engine sheared off a fan blade at cruising speed. Within milliseconds, the entire cowling disintegrated into flying shrapnel, puncturing the fuselage and blowing out a cabin window at row 14.

The cockpit erupted into instant chaos. Rapid decompression roared through the airframe, dropping cabin temperature below zero, flooding the cockpit with white vapor, and filling the air with deafening wind noise. The Boeing 737 shuddered violently, banking hard to 41 degrees with only one operational engine and zero internal communication back to the flight attendants.

In command was Captain Tammie Jo Shults, backed by First Officer Darren Ellisor.

Decades before flying commercial routes, Shults was breaking barriers in naval aviation as one of the first women to pilot the supersonic F/A-18 Hornet and fly tactical profiles in the A-7 Corsair II. She had spent years mastering emergency procedures on pitching carrier decks in pitch darkness, conditioning her nervous system to replace fear with immediate muscle memory.

While cockpit alarms blared and the airframe fought severe aerodynamic drag, Shults keyed her microphone to Philadelphia air traffic control. Her voice did not crack. Her cadence did not waver. She sounded like someone ordering a morning coffee.

"Southwest 1380 has an engine fire," she transmitted calmly. "We would like to descend."

When the controller asked whether the aircraft was actively on fire, her reply was cold steel.

"No, it is not on fire, but part of it is missing. They say there is a hole and someone went out."

Wrestling asymmetric thrust and flap damage, Shults manually stabilized the crippled airliner, brought it down on runway 27L at 165 knots, and safely delivered 148 souls home.

In September 2003, on her 3rd day in Iraq, Captain Kellie McCoy commanded a company from the 307th Engineers Battalion, 82nd Airborne. McCoy and 10 other soldiers set off on a convoy of 4 vehicles near Fallujah when they were ambushed with IEDs, automatic weapons, and RPGs. McCoy's humvee escaped serious damage, but the other 3 vehicles were disabled by the daisy-chain explosions. McCoy exited her vehicle and directed her soldiers toward her humvee. She returned fire at the ambushers, shooting two insurgents firing an RPG at the convoy. Most of her ammo was gone by the time she piled all 11 combat-loaded soldiers into her humvee and exited the kill zone. They returned to base with minor injuries, and no one was killed. For her outstanding role in directing the response of her column to the ambush and helping ensure everyone made it back alive, McCoy was awarded a Bronze Star with "V".

Microsoft has declared an internal "Code Red" inside its Microsoft 365 division after a historic 24-hour global outage on November 12–13 knocked out Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, according to internal memos obtained by Reuters (CTV News).

M365 Core President Jason Henderson told staff that "Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team" and admitted "Never before had so many customers been without email for so long" (MLQ.ai). Corporate VP Amanda Silver wrote that engineers worked through a "fog of war," trading more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats as they scrambled to restore service (Seeking Alpha).

Microsoft blamed the disruption on an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, ruled out cyberattacks or AI agents, and set a new target of deploying urgent fixes globally within one hour (The Next Web, Investing.com).
